claims.text: Structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by atomic-scale lattice distortions introduced by entropic mixing.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions slow atomic diffusion.
Slower atomic diffusion inhibits phase separation and compositional segregation.
The proposed high-entropy nanoalloys are initially homogeneously mixed.
The presence of multiple principal elements produces intrinsic lattice distortions in the proposed high-entropy nanoalloys.
Random and extensive elemental mixing causes atomic-scale lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys.
Lattice distortions raise local energy barriers for atomic hopping.
Raised atomic-hopping barriers reduce atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility minimizes grain growth during high-temperature exposure.
Reduced atomic mobility minimizes phase separation during high-temperature exposure.
Reduced atomic mobility minimizes chemical segregation during high-temperature exposure.
Relative to conventional nanoalloys, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit significantly less grain coarsening after annealing at 800–1000°C.
Relative to conventional nanoalloys, high-entropy nanoalloys will retain a more uniform chemical composition after annealing at 800–1000°C.
The prediction applies to nanoscale systems at 800–1000°C when diffusion is a dominant mechanism.
At substantially higher temperatures or in bulk materials, factors such as surface energy or oxidation may alter stability.
High-entropy and conventional nanoalloys should be annealed under identical controlled-atmosphere conditions and compared by grain size, phase composition, and elemental homogeneity.
Failure of the high-entropy nanoalloys to retain grain size and chemical homogeneity significantly better than conventional nanoalloys would falsify the stated hypothesis.
